What you will practice · Choose your pace

What you will practice

  • Narrow an audience brief while distinguishing the daily user, purchasing role, and evidence of need.
  • Negotiate a compelling comparative message without extending the comparison beyond the test.
  • Resolve ownership and release dependencies while separating a target date from authorization.
  • Give precise editorial feedback when a search-led article fails to deliver its stated promise.
  • Explain reported performance while resisting an unsupported claim of incremental impact.

Choose your pace

Quick practice · 15 minutes: complete one short exchange, check the explanations, and read both roles aloud.

Extended practice · two or three sittings: check the case facts, study the vocabulary and phrases, complete the longer conversation, then rehearse the follow-up exchange.

Level guide: designed for intermediate to advanced learners. B1 learners can start with the short exchanges and supplied phrases; B2 learners can complete the cloze conversations; C1 learners can focus on the distinctions in the language checks. 01Marketing Strategy: Audience, Insight, Problem, OutcomeThe scheduling tool with an audience of everyone+

Your goal

Narrow an audience brief while distinguishing the daily user, purchasing role, and evidence of need.

This lesson in the book, page 4 ↗

A Read the situation

The scheduling tool with an audience of everyone

A scheduling-software brief names the audience as "everyone who works in an office." Six exploratory interviews with operations coordinators at small agencies describe repeated calendar checking. No research with purchasing managers has been completed. The proposed campaign invites coordinators to book a workflow demonstration. A draft slide calls those six interviews proof of market-wide demand. Strategist Mira and product marketer Owen must revise the brief without inventing buyer research or promising that a demonstration request will become a sale.

Mira: Marketing strategist / Owen: Product marketer

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. Who was actually interviewed?

Answer and explanation

A. Six operations coordinators at small agencies

The briefing identifies a small exploratory user sample and explicitly excludes completed buyer research.

2. What does the proposed campaign ask people to do?

Answer and explanation

A. Book a workflow demonstration

The campaign action is a demonstration request, not a completed purchasing decision.

3. Which conclusion exceeds the evidence?

Answer and explanation

A. The interviews prove market-wide demand

Six exploratory interviews cannot establish the prevalence of a need across the whole market.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

An audience is not necessarily the buyer, and the buyer is not necessarily the person using the product daily. "Coordinators report repeated calendar checking" preserves the actual sample. "Office workers demand our product" changes both the population and the strength of the finding.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
target audience
The people a particular communication is intended to reach.define the target audience
market segment
A group distinguished by relevant shared needs or characteristics.prioritize a market segment
ideal customer profile
A description of organizations or customers considered a strong fit.refine the ideal customer profile
buyer persona
A research-informed representation of a purchasing role.validate a buyer persona
end user
The person who uses the product in practice.interview the end user
economic buyer
The role controlling the relevant purchasing budget.identify the economic buyer
buying committee
The group influencing or deciding an organizational purchase.map the buying committee
pain point
A specific problem the audience experiences.substantiate a pain point
customer insight
An interpretation that explains a meaningful customer pattern.develop a customer insight
jobs to be done
A framework focused on the progress people seek in a situation.frame the job to be done
use case
A concrete situation in which a product serves a need.define the primary use case
value proposition
The relevant benefit and reason to choose an offering.sharpen the value proposition
demand signal
Evidence suggesting interest or need, with limits.evaluate a demand signal
qualitative research
Research examining experiences and meaning rather than only numerical estimates.synthesize qualitative research
sample bias
Distortion arising from who is included in a sample.acknowledge sample bias
purchase trigger
An event or condition prompting buying consideration.identify a purchase trigger
decision criterion
A factor used to compare possible purchases.clarify the decision criteria
barrier to adoption
A condition that makes initial or continued use harder.investigate a barrier to adoption
addressable market
The market that could be served under a specified definition.define the addressable market
penetration
Adoption or participation relative to a defined market base.estimate market penetration
campaign objective
The particular outcome a campaign is intended to achieve.agree the campaign objective
conversion action
The defined behavior counted as a conversion.specify the conversion action
leading indicator
A measure that may precede a later outcome.monitor a leading indicator
research hypothesis
A testable proposition that still requires evidence.state a research hypothesis

An insight interprets evidence; a hypothesis proposes something to test. Neither word makes a small sample representative. A demonstration request can be a conversion action for this campaign while remaining only a possible step toward revenue.

C Notice the language

Challenge the scope without dismissing the ambition

A broad ambition can coexist with a focused first campaign. Use "for this campaign" to narrow the decision rather than imply that no other customer matters. Asking whose problem the message solves is more productive than labeling the brief vague and stopping there.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Narrow the decision
For this campaign, which role are we trying to reach first?
Preserve the research
The interviews involved six coordinators, not the entire office market.
Separate the roles
The daily user may not control the purchasing budget.
Define the action
We want qualified coordinators to book a workflow demonstration.
Name the problem
Repeated calendar checking is the reported friction.
Limit the inference
That is an exploratory signal, not proof of market-wide demand.
Request missing evidence
We still need to understand the purchasing manager's criteria.
Close with scope
Let us revise the audience, evidence statement, and conversion action.
Test the premise
We should label the buyer assumption as a hypothesis.
Clarify the benefit
Which part of the current workflow would the demonstration address?
Avoid a false trade-off
A focused first campaign does not rule out other segments later.
Define qualification
We need an agreed meaning of qualified before reporting those requests.
Check the wording
Does the slide distinguish what people said from our interpretation?
Locate the barrier
What prevents the user from trying the workflow?
Separate outcomes
A demonstration request is not the same as a completed sale.
Preserve uncertainty
We have a useful starting point, with buyer research still open.
6 language and precision notes
For this campaign
This phrase narrows a current decision without making a universal market claim.
Suggest versus prove
Suggest allows a bounded inference; prove claims much stronger support.
Audience and buyer
These labels name different roles even when one person fills both.
Qualified
State the criteria rather than treating the adjective as self-explanatory.
Reported friction
Reported attributes the problem to the research participants.
From request to sale
Naming both stages avoids treating an early action as final commercial success.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which revision preserves the research correctly?

Answer and explanation

C. Six interviewed coordinators described repeated calendar checking.

The supported statement retains the participants, observed problem, and limited scope.

2. Which question distinguishes use from purchasing authority?

Answer and explanation

A. Who uses the tool, and who controls the purchasing budget?

Daily use and budget authority can belong to different roles. Problem frequency, demonstration preferences and channel reach do not establish who can authorize a purchase.

3. Which label fits the immediate campaign action?

Answer and explanation

C. A booked workflow demonstration

The stated request is to book a demonstration, not complete the later stages.

4. Which response challenges the overclaim constructively?

Answer and explanation

B. Keep the insight, narrow its scope, and label the buyer assumption for research.

This response preserves useful evidence while correcting the unsupported generalization and missing buyer knowledge.

The scheduling tool with an audience of everyone

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Mira: Marketing strategist / Owen: Product marketer

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • end user
  • value proposition
  • leading indicator
  • buyer persona
  • target audience
  • pain point
  • research hypothesis
  • demand signal
  • market segment
  • conversion action
  1. Mira
    The brief says everyone who works in an office. I understand the ambition, but which person should recognize their own problem in the first campaign?
  2. Owen
    The clearest 1 is operations coordinators at small agencies. Six interviews described repeated calendar checking when colleagues tried to find a meeting time.
  3. Mira
    That gives us a starting point. Did those same people approve software purchases, or were they describing how they would use the product?
  4. Owen
    They spoke as the 2. We have not interviewed purchasing managers, so I cannot claim that the interviews establish who controls the budget.
  5. Mira
    Then the slide saying we have proved market-wide demand goes further than the research. Could we keep the finding but change its scope?
  6. Owen
    Yes. We have an exploratory 3, not a market estimate. I will keep the sample description next to the finding in the revised brief.
  7. Mira
    What are the coordinators actually struggling with? Give the creative team a concrete moment to show, not just the word scheduling.
  8. Owen
    The reported 4 is repeated calendar checking. We should demonstrate that workflow rather than promise to remove every administrative burden across an agency.
  9. Mira
    Good. What would we ask the coordinator to do after seeing the message? We need something more precise than engage with the brand.
  10. Owen
    Book a workflow demonstration. That is the proposed 5, but we still need agreed qualification criteria before calling every request a qualified opportunity.
  11. Mira
    A demonstration may interest the user without answering the purchasing manager's questions. We should avoid building that missing research into a confident buyer story.
  12. Owen
    Agreed. Our 6 remains incomplete. We can list the questions for research, but we should not invent purchasing priorities to make the brief look finished.
  13. Mira
    I expect someone will say the narrower audience limits growth. How can we explain this choice without suggesting that larger organizations will never matter?
  14. Owen
    Call it the initial 7. It is a focused campaign choice based on the evidence available, not a permanent boundary around the entire business.
  15. Mira
    The creative team also wants a single sentence describing why this matters. Can that connect the workflow problem with a relevant product benefit?
  16. Owen
    Yes, but the 8 should stay within demonstrated capabilities. A numerical time-saving claim would need its own evidence before we add it to the message.
  17. Mira
    And when the first requests arrive, we should not present the count as proof that the revenue target has already been reached.
  18. Owen
    Correct. It can serve as a 9. We would still need to follow the requests through qualification and the actual purchasing process.
  19. Mira
    I will narrow the brief and change the call to action to a demonstration request. Send me the unanswered purchasing questions for the research brief.
  20. Owen
    I will label each unsupported buyer assumption as a 10. That gives the next research round a clear purpose without weakening the evidence we already have.

Answers and explanations
  1. target audience Turn 2. The target audience specifies whom this campaign addresses; it is narrower than everyone working in an office.
  2. end user Turn 4. The end user performs the workflow; using software does not establish control over its purchasing budget.
  3. demand signal Turn 6. The interviews indicate a possible need but do not establish its prevalence throughout the wider market.
  4. pain point Turn 8. The pain point is the specific repeated calendar-checking problem, not an unsupported claim about every scheduling task.
  5. conversion action Turn 10. The conversion action is the defined response counted by this campaign; it is not automatically a sale.
  6. buyer persona Turn 12. The buyer persona should be grounded in purchasing-role research, which this case says has not yet been completed.
  7. market segment Turn 14. The segment defines the campaign's first focus; choosing it does not exclude all future expansion.
  8. value proposition Turn 16. The value proposition connects a relevant benefit to the audience; it must not import an unverified numerical claim.
  9. leading indicator Turn 18. A leading indicator may precede a later outcome; it does not establish that the later outcome occurred.
  10. research hypothesis Turn 20. A research hypothesis identifies a proposition to test rather than presenting it as an established customer fact.

Dialogue in the book, page 10 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

The scheduling buyer may not be the user

The lesson's scheduling-tool brief targets everyone in an office; the buyer and daily user have not been identified.

  1. Marketing strategist: The brief targets everyone who works in an office. Who actually buys this scheduling tool?
  2. Product manager: We haven't separated the buyer from the daily user, so that audience is too broad.
  3. Marketing strategist: Could we clarify whose problem the campaign needs to address before creating a persona?
  4. Product manager: Yes. A purchasing decision and a daily scheduling task may involve different people.
  5. Marketing strategist: Then an ideal customer profile, or ICP, shouldn't simply repeat everyone in an office.
  6. Product manager: Agreed. We need evidence about the relevant organization and the roles involved.
  7. Marketing strategist: What job to be done, or JTBD, should the research investigate first?
  8. Product manager: The actual scheduling difficulty. We haven't established which difficulty matters most, so let's ask rather than invent it.
  9. Marketing strategist: I'll separate segment, buyer, user, and unanswered problem questions in the discussion.
  10. Product manager: Good. We can define the campaign outcome once that audience understanding is clearer.
One signup list contains two different needs

Separate fictional research exercise: event signups include office managers seeking room booking and recruiters seeking interview coordination; purchasing authority is unknown.

  1. Demand generation lead: Can we treat this signup list as one persona because everyone requested scheduling information?
  2. Researcher: The stated needs differ: office managers mention room booking, while recruiters mention interview coordination.
  3. Demand generation lead: So the shared topic doesn't establish a shared job to be done.
  4. Researcher: Exactly. We should clarify the desired task and who participates in the purchase.
  5. Demand generation lead: Could we assume the office managers control budget because of their titles?
  6. Researcher: No. Purchasing authority hasn't been established for either group in this exercise.
  7. Demand generation lead: Then I'll ask which workflow each contact wants to improve before choosing the campaign message.
  8. Researcher: Also distinguish expressed interest from evidence that the segment matches our ideal customer profile.
  9. Demand generation lead: I'll keep the two stated needs separate and avoid inventing budget ownership.
  10. Researcher: Good. That gives us focused discovery questions instead of a persona built from job-title assumptions.
A productivity goal needs a named task

Separate fictional campaign intake: a team wants to promote a document tool as improving productivity, but no target task or desired behavior is specified.

  1. Campaign planner: When you say productivity, which task should the audience be able to complete more effectively?
  2. Product lead: We haven't chosen a task. The brief currently describes the entire document tool.
  3. Campaign planner: Then we need clarification before deciding on a segment or a useful outcome.
  4. Product lead: Could a broad message work until we have more detailed audience evidence?
  5. Campaign planner: It might be a hypothesis, but we shouldn't call it a validated value proposition.
  6. Product lead: What would you ask first in the research conversation with a potential user?
  7. Campaign planner: Which document task creates difficulty, and what would a successful result look like?
  8. Product lead: That would help distinguish a feature request from the job they actually need done.
  9. Campaign planner: Yes. We'll keep any persona provisional until the evidence supports a more specific description.
  10. Product lead: Let's clarify the task and outcome before asking creative to produce campaign concepts.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

The scheduling tool with an audience of everyone
  1. Read the corrected audience discussion. Preserve six coordinator interviews as exploratory evidence and distinguish the daily user from the purchasing role.
  2. Switch roles. Stress the proposed demo-booking action and the buyer research still missing; keep a demonstration request separate from a sale.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

The user is not the purchaser

A workplace-learning product is used by employees, but the learning director approves the purchase. A campaign invites employees to try a sample lesson; no company contract has been signed.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Strategist: "Employees are the daily ___."

Answer and explanation

A. users

The supplied facts identify employees as the people using the learning product.

2. Marketer: "The learning director controls the purchasing ___."

Answer and explanation

B. decision

The director approves the purchase, which differs from employees trying a lesson.

3. Strategist: "Trying a sample is the campaign's immediate ___."

Answer and explanation

A. action

The invitation asks for a sample trial rather than a completed company purchase.

4. Marketer: "We must not report that trial as a signed ___."

Answer and explanation

C. contract

No company contract has been signed, so the early behavior cannot be reported as one.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Build vocabulary and collocations — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Language workshop: The scheduling tool with an audience of everyone
Communication goal: Narrow an audience brief while distinguishing the daily user, purchasing role, and evidence of need.
Language guidance: An audience is not necessarily the buyer, and the buyer is not necessarily the person using the product daily. "Coordinators report repeated calendar checking" preserves the actual sample. "Office workers demand our product" changes both the population and the strength of the finding.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): For this campaign, which role are we trying to reach first? / The interviews involved six coordinators, not the entire office market. / The daily user may not control the purchasing budget. / We want qualified coordinators to book a workflow demonstration. / Repeated calendar checking is the reported friction. / That is an exploratory signal, not proof of market-wide demand. / We still need to understand the purchasing manager's criteria. / Let us revise the audience, evidence statement, and conversion action. / We should label the buyer assumption as a hypothesis. / Which part of the current workflow would the demonstration address? / A focused first campaign does not rule out other segments later. / We need an agreed meaning of qualified before reporting those requests. / Does the slide distinguish what people said from our interpretation? / What prevents the user from trying the workflow? / A demonstration request is not the same as a completed sale. / We have a useful starting point, with buyer research still open.
Vocabulary: target audience: The people a particular communication is intended to reach. / market segment: A group distinguished by relevant shared needs or characteristics. / ideal customer profile: A description of organizations or customers considered a strong fit. / buyer persona: A research-informed representation of a purchasing role. / end user: The person who uses the product in practice. / economic buyer: The role controlling the relevant purchasing budget. / buying committee: The group influencing or deciding an organizational purchase. / pain point: A specific problem the audience experiences. / customer insight: An interpretation that explains a meaningful customer pattern. / jobs to be done: A framework focused on the progress people seek in a situation. / use case: A concrete situation in which a product serves a need. / value proposition: The relevant benefit and reason to choose an offering. / demand signal: Evidence suggesting interest or need, with limits. / qualitative research: Research examining experiences and meaning rather than only numerical estimates. / sample bias: Distortion arising from who is included in a sample. / purchase trigger: An event or condition prompting buying consideration. / decision criterion: A factor used to compare possible purchases. / barrier to adoption: A condition that makes initial or continued use harder. / addressable market: The market that could be served under a specified definition. / penetration: Adoption or participation relative to a defined market base. / campaign objective: The particular outcome a campaign is intended to achieve. / conversion action: The defined behavior counted as a conversion. / leading indicator: A measure that may precede a later outcome. / research hypothesis: A testable proposition that still requires evidence.
Speaking task: Read the corrected audience discussion. Preserve six coordinator interviews as exploratory evidence and distinguish the daily user from the purchasing role. Switch roles. Keep employees as users and the learning director as purchase approver.

Lesson 01: Marketing Strategy: Audience, Insight, Problem, Outcome
Original fictional case: A scheduling-software brief names the audience as "everyone who works in an office." Six exploratory interviews with operations coordinators at small agencies describe repeated calendar checking. No research with purchasing managers has been completed. The proposed campaign invites coordinators to book a workflow demonstration. A draft slide calls those six interviews proof of market-wide demand. Strategist Mira and product marketer Owen must revise the brief without inventing buyer research or promising that a demonstration request will become a sale.
Language workshop: The scheduling tool with an audience of everyone
Communication goal: Narrow an audience brief while distinguishing the daily user, purchasing role, and evidence of need.
Language guidance: An audience is not necessarily the buyer, and the buyer is not necessarily the person using the product daily. "Coordinators report repeated calendar checking" preserves the actual sample. "Office workers demand our product" changes both the population and the strength of the finding.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): For this campaign, which role are we trying to reach first? / The interviews involved six coordinators, not the entire office market. / The daily user may not control the purchasing budget. / We want qualified coordinators to book a workflow demonstration. / Repeated calendar checking is the reported friction. / That is an exploratory signal, not proof of market-wide demand. / We still need to understand the purchasing manager's criteria. / Let us revise the audience, evidence statement, and conversion action. / We should label the buyer assumption as a hypothesis. / Which part of the current workflow would the demonstration address? / A focused first campaign does not rule out other segments later. / We need an agreed meaning of qualified before reporting those requests. / Does the slide distinguish what people said from our interpretation? / What prevents the user from trying the workflow? / A demonstration request is not the same as a completed sale. / We have a useful starting point, with buyer research still open.
Vocabulary: target audience: The people a particular communication is intended to reach. / market segment: A group distinguished by relevant shared needs or characteristics. / ideal customer profile: A description of organizations or customers considered a strong fit. / buyer persona: A research-informed representation of a purchasing role. / end user: The person who uses the product in practice. / economic buyer: The role controlling the relevant purchasing budget. / buying committee: The group influencing or deciding an organizational purchase. / pain point: A specific problem the audience experiences. / customer insight: An interpretation that explains a meaningful customer pattern. / jobs to be done: A framework focused on the progress people seek in a situation. / use case: A concrete situation in which a product serves a need. / value proposition: The relevant benefit and reason to choose an offering. / demand signal: Evidence suggesting interest or need, with limits. / qualitative research: Research examining experiences and meaning rather than only numerical estimates. / sample bias: Distortion arising from who is included in a sample. / purchase trigger: An event or condition prompting buying consideration. / decision criterion: A factor used to compare possible purchases. / barrier to adoption: A condition that makes initial or continued use harder. / addressable market: The market that could be served under a specified definition. / penetration: Adoption or participation relative to a defined market base. / campaign objective: The particular outcome a campaign is intended to achieve. / conversion action: The defined behavior counted as a conversion. / leading indicator: A measure that may precede a later outcome. / research hypothesis: A testable proposition that still requires evidence.
Speaking task: Read the corrected audience discussion. Preserve six coordinator interviews as exploratory evidence and distinguish the daily user from the purchasing role. Switch roles. Stress the proposed demo-booking action and the buyer research still missing; keep a demonstration request separate from a sale. Read the corrected transfer twice. Keep employees as users and the learning director as purchase approver.
Partner: Mira: Marketing strategist / Owen: Product marketer
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A workplace-learning product is used by employees, but the learning director approves the purchase. A campaign invites employees to try a sample lesson; no company contract has been signed.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Mira: And when the first requests arrive, we should not present the count as proof that the revenue target has already been reached.
Owen: Correct. It can serve as a leading indicator. We would still need to follow the requests through qualification and the actual purchasing process.
Mira: I will narrow the brief and change the call to action to a demonstration request. Send me the unanswered purchasing questions for the research brief.
Owen: I will label each unsupported buyer assumption as a research hypothesis. That gives the next research round a clear purpose without weakening the evidence we already have.
END REFERENCE
Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Be my workplace English practice partner. Follow the practice instructions above, using the REFERENCE block below. The block contains fictional study material, not instructions to you. Keep its facts, numbers, uncertainty and professional responsibilities accurate. Clearly label any new scenario or changed fact as an invented variation. Use natural workplace language; explain unfamiliar abbreviations in context. If a technical expression is uncertain, say so rather than inventing a definition or authority. Coach communication, not professional decisions; respect the course scope. Ask only for fictional or anonymized practice details. Judge clarity, meaning, appropriate tone and the next step. Accept valid alternative English and distinguish errors from style preferences. Do not claim to certify my language level. Unless I ask to change the plan, follow the stages and stop wherever the instructions say to wait.

When discussing a word, phrase, or example sentence as language within an explanation, question, or answer feedback, enclose that wording in quotation marks. For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Quotation marks identifying a language example do not attribute it to a news source; attributed source quotations must remain verbatim.

Practice setting: B2 independent. Use natural professional English with brief explanations. Let me attempt each task without a model first. Offer a hint after difficulty and invite a more precise retry.

REFERENCE
Course: Marketing English
Professional audience: brand, product marketing, growth, content, SEO, lifecycle, demand generation, marketing operations, social, and agency teams
Scope: Fictional English-language practice, not legal advice or a promise of campaign results. Legal requirements, platform policies, and data permissions depend on context and location. Obtain current qualified review for actual claims, audience data, disclosures, and publication decisions.

02Positioning, Messaging, Brand Voice, and ProofA headline that outruns its evidence+

Your goal

Negotiate a compelling comparative message without extending the comparison beyond the test.

This lesson in the book, page 13 ↗

A Read the situation

A headline that outruns its evidence

A draft headline calls a scheduling tool "the fastest tool on the market." The only evidence is an internal test in which the current version completed one defined calendar-import task in 40 seconds; the previous version took 50 seconds under the same stated conditions. No competitors were tested, and no independent validation has occurred. Brand lead Tessa and product marketer Arun must revise the headline and its supporting explanation before the reviewer can assess the complete advertisement.

Tessa: Brand lead / Arun: Product marketer

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What was the actual comparator?

Answer and explanation

D. The previous version of the same product

The briefing describes a version-to-version internal task test with no competitor comparison.

2. What time reduction does the supplied test show?

Answer and explanation

B. 10 seconds, or 20% of the previous 50 seconds

The reduction is 50 minus 40 seconds; dividing 10 by the original 50 gives 20%.

3. Which statement is unsupported?

Answer and explanation

B. The product is the fastest on the market

A market-wide superlative cannot be established by a test against only the product's earlier version.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Time falls 20%: (50 - 40) / 50. The reciprocal task rate rises 25%: (50 / 40) - 1. State the measured quantity, task, comparator and conditions rather than using ambiguous faster wording. Neither calculation establishes a market ranking or every customer workflow.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
positioning
How an offering is framed relative to audience needs and alternatives.clarify the positioning
message hierarchy
The order of importance assigned to communication points.build a message hierarchy
headline
The main line introducing an advertisement or article.revise the headline
supporting copy
Text developing or qualifying the main message.align the supporting copy
proof point
Specific evidence supporting a proposition.attach a proof point
substantiation
Evidence that supports an objective advertising claim.review claim substantiation
comparative claim
A statement comparing an offering with something else.qualify a comparative claim
superlative
A strongest-ranking expression such as fastest or largest.challenge an unsupported superlative
comparator
The product, group, or baseline used for comparison.identify the comparator
test conditions
The circumstances under which a test was conducted.disclose relevant test conditions
benchmark
A reference measure or defined test for comparison.document the benchmark
claim scope
The range of circumstances a claim purports to cover.narrow the claim scope
qualifier
Wording that limits or specifies a statement's meaning.retain the necessary qualifier
net impression
The overall message an audience takes from an advertisement.review the net impression
brand voice
The relatively consistent verbal personality of a brand.preserve the brand voice
tone
The attitude expressed in a specific communication.adjust the tone
reason to believe
Support that makes a promised benefit credible.supply a reason to believe
differentiator
A relevant feature or benefit distinguishing an offering.substantiate the differentiator
benefit statement
Wording describing a useful outcome for the audience.sharpen the benefit statement
feature claim
A statement about a product's capability or characteristic.verify a feature claim
message architecture
An organized structure of core and supporting messages.maintain the message architecture
creative territory
A broad conceptual direction for creative work.explore a creative territory
copy review
Assessment of wording and its implications before use.complete the copy review
approval status
The recorded state of an item's review and authorization.confirm the approval status

A footnote does not automatically repair a headline that gives the wrong overall impression. The complete advertisement needs review. A marketer can prepare a narrower candidate statement without claiming that the reviewer has already approved it.

C Notice the language

Defend the proposition, not a favorite adjective

Creative review can feel personal when a team has invested in a line. Acknowledge the intended effect, name the evidence problem, and propose a narrower proposition. This keeps the discussion about the communication task rather than the writer's ability or enthusiasm.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Recognize the aim
The line creates energy, but its comparison is broader than the test.
Name the comparator
We tested the current version against our previous version.
Bound the result
The task took 40 seconds rather than 50 in this internal test.
State the calculation
That is a 20% reduction in the measured task time.
Reject the extension
We have no competitor evidence for a market-wide ranking.
Offer a revision
Let us build the message around the specific tested improvement.
Preserve the context
Keep the task and conditions with the claim.
Close with review
The complete revised advertisement still needs approval.
Separate style and fact
We can keep a confident tone without adding an unsupported superlative.
Check the impression
Would a reader infer a broader performance promise?
Avoid shorthand
I would say reduced task time, not simply faster everywhere.
Name the evidence gap
Independent validation is not part of the supplied evidence.
Mark the version
Please attach the exact tested build and test record.
Protect the benefit
The useful story is the improvement in this defined workflow.
Clarify authority
This is proposed wording, not final clearance.
Request a decision
Can we agree the proposition before polishing the headline?
6 language and precision notes
Compared with
This expression should identify the actual reference, not leave a reader to assume competitors.
By and to
Time fell by 10 seconds, to 40 seconds; these prepositions encode different values.
Percent and seconds
Give the original basis when converting an absolute change to a percentage.
Confident tone
Verbal confidence does not require a universal factual claim.
Proposed wording
Proposed preserves the distinction between a candidate and an approved advertisement.
Overall impression
Review how headline, image, and qualifiers work together, not just isolated sentences.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which claim most closely matches the supplied measurement?

Answer and explanation

B. The defined task took 20% less time than in the previous version under the test conditions.

The supported comparison retains the measured task, time basis, earlier version, and conditions.

2. Which sentence uses by and to accurately?

Answer and explanation

C. Task time fell by 10 seconds to 40 seconds.

The measured values are 50 seconds originally and 40 seconds afterward, a difference of 10.

3. What does the proposed revised wording still require?

Answer and explanation

C. Review of the complete advertisement and supporting evidence

Arithmetic, a comparator note and creative agreement do not by themselves establish the overall message or approval. The full advertisement must be assessed with its evidence.

4. Which feedback is most useful?

Answer and explanation

C. Preserve the benefit, but narrow the comparator and task scope.

The useful revision retains a meaningful tested improvement without expanding or mislabeling the evidence.

E Conversations

A headline that outruns its evidence

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Tessa: Brand lead / Arun: Product marketer

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • net impression
  • claim scope
  • brand voice
  • substantiation
  • approval status
  • qualifier
  • benchmark
  • supporting copy
  • comparator
  • proof point
  1. Tessa
    The creative team likes the fastest tool on the market. It is short and energetic, but I want to check exactly what supports it.
  2. Arun
    The available 1 is our previous version. We tested one calendar-import task, and we have not tested competing tools or obtained independent validation.
  3. Tessa
    So fastest on the market suggests a ranking we have not established. What numbers can we actually put behind a narrower statement?
  4. Arun
    The 2 recorded fifty seconds for the previous version and forty for the current one under the same stated conditions. The difference is ten seconds.
  5. Tessa
    That is twenty percent less task time, using fifty as the original base. I would avoid saying customers save twenty percent of their day.
  6. Arun
    Right. The 3 should cover that task and comparison. It does not cover every workflow, every customer, or every configuration in which the product might run.
  7. Tessa
    Could the headline simply say twenty percent faster and leave the explanation underneath? I am concerned that we are losing the useful benefit.
  8. Arun
    I would retain the measurement in the 4 and develop a headline that does not change it. Less time for this task is clearer than an unqualified speed promise.
  9. Tessa
    The team may suggest putting a small asterisk after fastest. Would that solve the problem if the footnote names our previous version?
  10. Arun
    Not automatically. The 5 could still be a market-wide ranking. We need the reviewer to assess the whole advertisement, rather than assume an asterisk fixes the headline.
  11. Tessa
    I accept that fastest on the market goes too far. Can we give the writer a sharper direction than simply adding another footnote?
  12. Arun
    We can preserve the 6. The confidence can come from a specific improvement and clear evidence, without the unsupported claim that no competitor is quicker.
  13. Tessa
    Then let us agree the proposition first: the new version reduced the measured calendar-import time compared with our old version in this test.
  14. Arun
    That gives us a concrete 7. I will attach the test record so the reviewer can check the exact task, build, and conditions behind the wording.
  15. Tessa
    Can we call the result independently verified once the reviewer checks the copy, or would that imply a different kind of testing?
  16. Arun
    It would imply evidence we do not have. Internal copy approval does not become independent 8 of the test result. We should describe the evidence as internal.
  17. Tessa
    I will ask for two tighter headline options around that proposition. Neither should suggest a universal benefit or comparison with the entire market.
  18. Arun
    And each necessary 9 must stay visible where it matters. Otherwise the shorter version may communicate something different from the result we actually measured.
  19. Tessa
    I will ask for two new headlines and a complete mock-up. Keep the current version out of the release folder until the reviewer has seen it.
  20. Arun
    Exactly. I will mark its 10 as pending and keep the evidence attached. We should not release a fragment just because we agreed on the direction today.

Answers and explanations
  1. comparator Turn 2. The comparator was the previous version; no competing products were included in the stated test.
  2. benchmark Turn 4. The benchmark is the defined task comparison with recorded times, not evidence of a market-wide ranking.
  3. claim scope Turn 6. Claim scope defines what the statement covers; a single task test cannot establish all customer time savings.
  4. supporting copy Turn 8. Supporting copy develops the headline, but its task-time explanation must remain consistent with the main message.
  5. net impression Turn 10. The overall impression may still imply market superiority even when a small note names a narrower comparison.
  6. brand voice Turn 12. Brand voice concerns how the brand speaks; it does not justify adding an unsupported factual ranking.
  7. proof point Turn 14. The proof point is the bounded recorded improvement, not a prediction of every user's experience.
  8. substantiation Turn 16. Substantiation supports the factual claim; an internal wording review does not transform an internal test into independent validation.
  9. qualifier Turn 18. A qualifier preserves the task, comparator, or conditions that limit what the evidence supports.
  10. approval status Turn 20. Approval status distinguishes a proposed revision from a version authorized for publication after the complete review.

  5. Tessa: That is twenty percent less task time, using fifty as the original base. I would avoid saying customers save twenty percent of their day.
  6. Arun: Right. The claim scope should cover that task and comparison. It does not cover every workflow, every customer, or every configuration in which the product might run.
  7. Tessa: Could the headline simply say twenty percent faster and leave the explanation underneath? I am concerned that we are losing the useful benefit.
  8. Arun: I would retain the measurement in the supporting copy and develop a headline that does not change it. Less time for this task is clearer than an unqualified speed promise.
  9. Tessa: The team may suggest putting a small asterisk after fastest. Would that solve the problem if the footnote names our previous version?
  10. Arun: Not automatically. The net impression could still be a market-wide ranking. We need the reviewer to assess the whole advertisement, rather than assume an asterisk fixes the headline.
  11. Tessa: I accept that fastest on the market goes too far. Can we give the writer a sharper direction than simply adding another footnote?
  12. Arun: We can preserve the brand voice. The confidence can come from a specific improvement and clear evidence, without the unsupported claim that no competitor is quicker.
  13. Tessa: Then let us agree the proposition first: the new version reduced the measured calendar-import time compared with our old version in this test.
  14. Arun: That gives us a concrete proof point. I will attach the test record so the reviewer can check the exact task, build, and conditions behind the wording.

Dialogue in the book, page 19 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

An earlier-version test cannot prove fastest in market

Separate fictional extension of the lesson: an internal test exported the same 100-row report in eight seconds on the new version and ten on the earlier version, on the same test machine. No market-wide or other-task comparison exists.

  1. Copywriter: The headline says fastest tool on the market. Our proof point is an internal comparison with the earlier version.
  2. Brand reviewer: That test doesn't cover the whole market, so the positioning claim exceeds the evidence.
  3. Copywriter: Could we say faster than our earlier version instead, with the test conditions visible?
  4. Brand reviewer: Only within what the test actually measured. We shouldn't imply every task or environment improved.
  5. Copywriter: Then the brand promise needs to be narrower than the ambitious headline I drafted.
  6. Brand reviewer: Yes. Clear qualification can preserve a useful message without pretending a broader comparison occurred.
  7. Copywriter: I'll propose: In our internal 100-row report-export test, the new version took eight seconds versus ten previously.
  8. Brand reviewer: Good. Keep the actual test reference available to whoever checks that wording.
  9. Copywriter: We can develop a value proposition around the supported benefit rather than a market-wide superlative.
  10. Brand reviewer: Exactly. The revised claim should tell readers what was tested, not what we hope is true.
Three customer quotes are not universal experience

Separate fictional messaging review: three interviewees describe a tool as easy to learn; no broader usability study exists.

  1. Brand manager: Three interviewees said the tool was easy to learn. Can our message say anyone masters it immediately?
  2. Customer researcher: No. Those comments describe three experiences, not a universal learning outcome or measured completion time.
  3. Brand manager: Could we use the comments as a proof point without turning them into that promise?
  4. Customer researcher: We can consider accurately attributed feedback, subject to the relevant use review and context.
  5. Brand manager: We haven't measured how long learning took, so immediately would add an unsupported fact.
  6. Customer researcher: Correct. And anyone would extend three accounts to every potential user.
  7. Brand manager: I'll propose wording that describes the interview feedback rather than guarantees mastery.
  8. Customer researcher: Please retain the limited sample and avoid presenting the interviews as a comprehensive study.
  9. Brand manager: That still supports a discussion about accessible onboarding while keeping the brand promise honest.
  10. Customer researcher: Yes. Then further research can test whether the broader positioning is justified.
A feature exists, but the benefit is unmeasured

Separate fictional launch: a product adds reusable templates; no measured time-saving study has been conducted.

  1. Product marketer: We now have reusable templates. Can the value proposition promise to cut preparation time in half?
  2. Product manager: The feature exists, but we haven't measured that time-saving claim in a study.
  3. Product marketer: Then the capability is observed, while the fifty-percent benefit is only an unsupported assumption.
  4. Product manager: Exactly. We can explain that users can reuse a template without inventing the resulting savings.
  5. Product marketer: How about create a template once and reuse it for later documents?
  6. Product manager: That describes the supplied capability, provided the final wording matches the feature's actual scope.
  7. Product marketer: I'll take that wording for review and remove the numerical promise.
  8. Product manager: Good. A brand promise should not turn a plausible benefit into a measured proof point.
  9. Product marketer: We can propose a later task-based study if we want to quantify the benefit.
  10. Product manager: Yes. Until then, capability and measured outcome should remain separate in our messaging.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

A headline that outruns its evidence
  1. Read the corrected claim review. State 50 seconds down to 40, ten seconds less and a 20% time reduction against the previous version.
  2. Switch roles. Keep the internal task test distinct from independent validation and competitor ranking; retain the need to review the full advertisement.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A larger sample, not a wider claim

A packaging team tests one box design with 80 participants. Sixty choose it over the old design. No competing brands appear, and the sample is not established as representative.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Researcher: "Sixty out of eighty is ___ percent."

Answer and explanation

C. seventy-five

Dividing 60 by 80 gives 0.75, or 75 percent of the stated participants.

2. Marketer: "The ___ was our old design."

Answer and explanation

A. comparator

The test compared the two internal designs, not any competing brand.

3. Researcher: "Keep the participant ___ attached to the result."

Answer and explanation

B. sample

The limited, unverified sample cannot be silently expanded into a market-wide preference.

4. Marketer: "We cannot call this proof of market ___."

Answer and explanation

D. leadership

No competitor comparison or representative market ranking was established by the supplied test.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Build vocabulary and collocations — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Course: Marketing English
Professional audience: brand, product marketing, growth, content, SEO, lifecycle, demand generation, marketing operations, social, and agency teams

Lesson 02: Positioning, Messaging, Brand Voice, and Proof
Original fictional case: A draft headline calls a scheduling tool "the fastest tool on the market." The only evidence is an internal test in which the current version completed one defined calendar-import task in 40 seconds; the previous version took 50 seconds under the same stated conditions. No competitors were tested, and no independent validation has occurred. Brand lead Tessa and product marketer Arun must revise the headline and its supporting explanation before the reviewer can assess the complete advertisement.
Language workshop: A headline that outruns its evidence
Communication goal: Negotiate a compelling comparative message without extending the comparison beyond the test.
Language guidance: Time falls 20%: (50 - 40) / 50. The reciprocal task rate rises 25%: (50 / 40) - 1. State the measured quantity, task, comparator and conditions rather than using ambiguous faster wording. Neither calculation establishes a market ranking or every customer workflow.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The line creates energy, but its comparison is broader than the test. / We tested the current version against our previous version. / The task took 40 seconds rather than 50 in this internal test. / That is a 20% reduction in the measured task time. / We have no competitor evidence for a market-wide ranking. / Let us build the message around the specific tested improvement. / Keep the task and conditions with the claim. / The complete revised advertisement still needs approval. / We can keep a confident tone without adding an unsupported superlative. / Would a reader infer a broader performance promise? / I would say reduced task time, not simply faster everywhere. / Independent validation is not part of the supplied evidence. / Please attach the exact tested build and test record. / The useful story is the improvement in this defined workflow. / This is proposed wording, not final clearance. / Can we agree the proposition before polishing the headline?
Vocabulary: positioning: How an offering is framed relative to audience needs and alternatives. / message hierarchy: The order of importance assigned to communication points. / headline: The main line introducing an advertisement or article. / supporting copy: Text developing or qualifying the main message. / proof point: Specific evidence supporting a proposition. / substantiation: Evidence that supports an objective advertising claim. / comparative claim: A statement comparing an offering with something else. / superlative: A strongest-ranking expression such as fastest or largest. / comparator: The product, group, or baseline used for comparison. / test conditions: The circumstances under which a test was conducted. / benchmark: A reference measure or defined test for comparison. / claim scope: The range of circumstances a claim purports to cover. / qualifier: Wording that limits or specifies a statement's meaning. / net impression: The overall message an audience takes from an advertisement. / brand voice: The relatively consistent verbal personality of a brand. / tone: The attitude expressed in a specific communication. / reason to believe: Support that makes a promised benefit credible. / differentiator: A relevant feature or benefit distinguishing an offering. / benefit statement: Wording describing a useful outcome for the audience. / feature claim: A statement about a product's capability or characteristic. / message architecture: An organized structure of core and supporting messages. / creative territory: A broad conceptual direction for creative work. / copy review: Assessment of wording and its implications before use. / approval status: The recorded state of an item's review and authorization.
Speaking task: Read the corrected claim review. State 50 seconds down to 40, ten seconds less and a 20% time reduction against the previous version. Switch roles. Keep the internal task test distinct from independent validation and competitor ranking; retain the need to review the full advertisement. Read the corrected transfer. Report 60 of 80 participants as 75% without converting design preference into market leadership.
Partner: Tessa: Brand lead / Arun: Product marketer
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A packaging team tests one box design with 80 participants. Sixty choose it over the old design. No competing brands appear, and the sample is not established as representative.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Tessa: I will ask for two tighter headline options around that proposition. Neither should suggest a universal benefit or comparison with the entire market.
Arun: And each necessary qualifier must stay visible where it matters. Otherwise the shorter version may communicate something different from the result we actually measured.
Tessa: I will ask for two new headlines and a complete mock-up. Keep the current version out of the release folder until the reviewer has seen it.
Arun: Exactly. I will mark its approval status as pending and keep the evidence attached. We should not release a fragment just because we agreed on the direction today.
END REFERENCE

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.
