06Lifecycle, CRM, Email, Marketing Ops, and Sales HandoffA hundred contacts are not a hundred sales requests+

Your goal

Clarify lifecycle status and routing rules without turning activity records into invented buying intent.

This lesson in the book, page 49 ↗

A Read the situation

A hundred contacts are not a hundred sales requests

A campaign export contains 100 contacts: 20 submitted a demonstration request, 60 downloaded a guide, and 20 have no recorded source. Contact permissions and suppression status have not been checked. The company's stated handoff procedure requires a verified source, a documented sales request, completed permission checks, and a named owner before a record is routed as sales-ready. Marketing-operations specialist Jules and sales-development lead Nico must correct an email calling all 100 contacts ready for sales outreach.

Jules: Marketing-operations specialist / Nico: Sales-development lead

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. How many contacts have a documented demonstration request?

Answer and explanation

C. 20

The supplied export separates 20 demonstration requests from 60 guide downloads and 20 unknown-source records.

2. What remains unchecked across the export?

Answer and explanation

A. Contact permissions and suppression status

The briefing explicitly says permission and suppression checks have not yet been completed.

3. Can all 100 records currently be called sales-ready under the stated procedure?

Answer and explanation

D. No; the request, source, checks, and ownership conditions are not all met.

The company's supplied criteria require more than contact details, and the case does not impose a blanket ban on responding.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

A downloaded guide is a recorded action, not a stated request for a sales conversation. Qualification labels are organization-specific. This case supplies its own handoff conditions; do not replace them with an assumed universal meaning of MQL or SQL.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
CRM
Customer relationship management system or practice for relationship records.update the CRM record
lifecycle stage
A defined position in a contact's relationship with the organization.verify the lifecycle stage
lead
A potential customer record whose qualification depends on agreed criteria.review a new lead
marketing-qualified lead
A lead meeting the organization's stated marketing qualification criteria.define a marketing-qualified lead
sales-qualified lead
A lead meeting the organization's stated sales qualification criteria.confirm a sales-qualified lead
lead scoring
Applying defined values to attributes or behavior to prioritize leads.calibrate lead scoring
fit score
A score representing alignment with the target customer profile.review the fit score
intent signal
Behavior suggesting interest without necessarily proving a buying decision.interpret an intent signal
lead source
The recorded origin of a contact or lead.verify the lead source
source provenance
The traceable history of how data was obtained.preserve source provenance
consent record
A record of permission with relevant scope and context.check the consent record
suppression list
Records excluded from specified communication activity.apply the suppression list
unsubscribe
A request or action to stop a type of communication.process an unsubscribe
preference center
A place where recipients manage communication choices.update the preference center
double opt-in
A process confirming a subscription through a second action.document the double opt-in
deliverability
The ability of messages to reach their intended inbox destination.monitor deliverability
hard bounce
A delivery failure generally indicating a persistent address problem.suppress a hard bounce
soft bounce
A delivery failure often associated with a temporary condition.investigate a soft bounce
nurture sequence
A planned series of communications supporting a relationship over time.review the nurture sequence
triggered email
A message initiated by a defined event or condition.test the triggered email
segmentation rule
A criterion used to assign records to an audience group.validate a segmentation rule
routing rule
A condition determining which owner receives a record or task.apply the routing rule
service-level agreement
An agreement defining service responsibilities and response expectations.clarify the service-level agreement
recycle reason
A recorded explanation for returning a lead to an earlier process stage.document the recycle reason

A permission record needs context such as channel, purpose, and status. Do not infer universal legal permission or prohibition from the presence of an address. Apply the supplied company procedure and obtain qualified review of the actual jurisdictions and communication types.

C Notice the language

A shared label needs a shared threshold

Sales and marketing may use the same word for different stages. Ask what event and checks the label represents before debating lead quality. This keeps the discussion factual and avoids blaming either team for a handoff whose rules were never applied consistently.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Correct the count
Twenty contacts requested demonstrations; the other records have different statuses.
Separate actions
A guide download is not a documented sales request.
Name the missing check
Permissions and suppression status remain unverified.
Apply the threshold
Use the stated handoff criteria before marking a record sales-ready.
Preserve the source
Keep the original event and source history in the CRM.
Assign an owner
Each eligible handoff needs a named receiving owner.
Avoid an invented status
Unknown source should remain unknown until verified.
Close with routing
Route the verified requests through the agreed process.
Clarify the label
What conditions does qualified represent in this workflow?
Keep checks distinct
A demonstration request does not erase a separate suppression check.
Limit the batch
Do not describe the entire export as a single audience.
Check scope
Does the permission record cover this channel and purpose?
Request the trail
Please attach the source event and current status.
Explain a return
Use a specific recycle reason rather than simply rejecting the lead.
Protect the record
Do not overwrite the original source to make the export look complete.
Measure the handoff
Count records that meet the criteria, not every row in the file.
6 language and precision notes
Requested versus downloaded
These verbs describe different actions and must not be treated as interchangeable intent.
Qualified for what
A label needs the next action and applicable threshold.
Unknown versus absent
An unknown permission status is not evidence of either permission or a confirmed opt-out.
Pending checks
This phrase records an unfinished process without inventing its eventual result.
Every row versus eligible records
The denominator changes when a report filters by handoff conditions.
Company procedure
The supplied operational rule is not a statement of all jurisdictions' legal requirements.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which handoff summary is accurate?

Answer and explanation

A. Twenty demonstration requests are identified, with required checks still pending.

The summary preserves the known request count and does not invent results for the unfinished checks.

2. Which action preserves record integrity?

Answer and explanation

A. Retain the original source and mark unverified fields for review.

Source history and uncertainty should remain visible rather than be overwritten to satisfy a target.

3. Which record fits every stated sales-ready condition?

Answer and explanation

A. A documented request with verified source, completed permission checks and a named owner

The case requires the request, verified origin, permission checks and receiving owner together. Each alternative omits at least one condition or substitutes an engagement signal for a request.

4. Which question resolves a qualification disagreement?

Answer and explanation

A. Which event and completed checks does this stage require?

Asking for the stage's concrete criteria turns an ambiguous label into a testable operational definition.

Check explanations in the book, page 95 ↗

E Conversations

A hundred contacts are not a hundred sales requests

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Jules: Marketing-operations specialist / Nico: Sales-development lead

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • intent signal
  • source provenance
  • lifecycle stage
  • routing rule
  • recycle reason
  • lead source
  • consent record
  • service-level agreement
  • CRM
  • suppression list
  1. Nico
    The campaign email says we have one hundred sales-ready contacts. Before my team starts outreach, can you show me what those people actually requested?
  2. Jules
    The 1 export has twenty demonstration requests, sixty guide downloads, and twenty records with no source. Those are three different situations, not one consistent sales-ready group.
  3. Nico
    The downloaders have shown interest, though. Could we describe that as enough intent for a sales call and route them with the demonstration requests?
  4. Jules
    A download is an 2, but it is not the documented sales request our procedure requires. We should preserve what happened rather than strengthen the event's meaning.
  5. Nico
    That makes sense. What about the twenty people who explicitly asked for a demonstration? Are their records ready to assign now?
  6. Jules
    Their 3 is recorded, but permissions and suppression status have not been checked. The request does not by itself complete every condition in the handoff procedure.
  7. Nico
    Those twenty people asked for a demo; I do not want them forgotten. Can you flag the checks still needed and give each request an owner?
  8. Jules
    Yes. Keep the 4 accurate, with the missing checks visible. A pending state should tell the next colleague what remains, not become a place where requests disappear.
  9. Nico
    For the permission check, should we look only for a yes or no field? Some contacts have older records from another campaign.
  10. Jules
    Review the 5 with its channel, purpose, and status. An old flag without context is not a complete answer for this particular communication.
  11. Nico
    And if a current suppression record is present, the team should not assume the new export has somehow removed that restriction.
  12. Jules
    Correct. Apply the relevant 6 through the approved process. We should resolve any apparent conflict through review, not silently overwrite the status to increase the handoff count.
  13. Nico
    Once a request meets the criteria, I need it assigned to a specific person. Otherwise both teams may assume the other one is responding.
  14. Jules
    The 7 should identify that owner and preserve the source event. I will include the completed checks so the receiving colleague does not have to reconstruct the history.
  15. Nico
    We also need to agree how quickly eligible requests are acknowledged. That is a different conversation from inventing a deadline for unchecked records.
  16. Jules
    We can record it in the 8. The agreement should name the responsible team and what happens if the record is incomplete, rather than hide those cases in an average.
  17. Nico
    Suppose sales returns a record because the requested topic is outside our service. A generic rejection makes it hard to improve the next campaign.
  18. Jules
    Use a specific 9. That distinguishes a scope mismatch from missing information or an unanswered request without blaming the contact or changing the original event.
  19. Nico
    I will correct the hundred-sales-ready claim now. Send me the status of the twenty demo requests and keep the downloaders and unknown sources separate.
  20. Jules
    I will keep the 10 intact and investigate the unknown sources. We will count completed eligible handoffs, not relabel all one hundred rows to meet the campaign headline.

Answers and explanations
  1. CRM Turn 2. The CRM holds the relationship records, including the different events that produced this export.
  2. intent signal Turn 4. An intent signal can suggest interest without establishing the specific sales-conversation request required by this company's procedure.
  3. lead source Turn 6. The recorded demonstration-request source is one criterion, but permission, suppression, and ownership checks are separate requirements.
  4. lifecycle stage Turn 8. The lifecycle stage must reflect the current process state rather than prematurely label an unchecked record sales-ready.
  5. consent record Turn 10. A consent record needs scope and context; an older permission entry may not answer the current channel or purpose question.
  6. suppression list Turn 12. A suppression list excludes records from specified communication activity; exporting a record does not remove that status.
  7. routing rule Turn 14. A routing rule determines the receiving owner after the record meets the applicable handoff conditions.
  8. service-level agreement Turn 16. The service-level agreement defines responsibilities and response expectations rather than supplying missing qualification evidence.
  9. recycle reason Turn 18. A recycle reason explains why the record returns to an earlier process, making the handoff outcome usable for follow-up.
  10. source provenance Turn 20. Source provenance preserves how each record originated, including the unresolved history of unknown-source contacts.

  13. Nico: Once a request meets the criteria, I need it assigned to a specific person. Otherwise both teams may assume the other one is responding.
  14. Jules: The routing rule should identify that owner and preserve the source event. I will include the completed checks so the receiving colleague does not have to reconstruct the history.
  15. Nico: We also need to agree how quickly eligible requests are acknowledged. That is a different conversation from inventing a deadline for unchecked records.
  16. Jules: We can record it in the service-level agreement. The agreement should name the responsible team and what happens if the record is incomplete, rather than hide those cases in an average.
  17. Nico: Suppose sales returns a record because the requested topic is outside our service. A generic rejection makes it hard to improve the next campaign.
  18. Jules: Use a specific recycle reason. That distinguishes a scope mismatch from missing information or an unanswered request without blaming the contact or changing the original event.
  19. Nico: I will correct the hundred-sales-ready claim now. Send me the status of the twenty demo requests and keep the downloaders and unknown sources separate.
  20. Jules: I will keep the source provenance intact and investigate the unknown sources. We will count completed eligible handoffs, not relabel all one hundred rows to meet the campaign headline.
Dialogue in the book, page 55 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Contacts are not confirmed requests for calls

The lesson's lead list contains contact details but does not identify who requested a conversation.

  1. Marketing operations lead: The contact list is ready, but it doesn't identify which people requested a sales conversation.
  2. Sales development manager: Then I can't treat every record as an SQL ready for direct follow-up.
  3. Marketing operations lead: Correct. We need the qualification and contact-request context before making that handoff claim.
  4. Sales development manager: Does an MQL label in the list establish that a person asked to speak with us?
  5. Marketing operations lead: Not without checking our definitions and the recorded activity. The label alone isn't enough.
  6. Sales development manager: Please separate verified requests from records whose follow-up basis is unresolved.
  7. Marketing operations lead: I'll request that evidence and check the relevant suppression-list status through our process.
  8. Sales development manager: I'll hold off treating the unresolved group as confirmed conversation requests.
  9. Marketing operations lead: Could you confirm what you need to accept the corrected handoff?
  10. Sales development manager: The request evidence, qualification context, and applicable contact restrictions, with unknowns clearly marked.
A nurture handoff needs the actual last interaction

Separate fictional lifecycle exercise: three contacts attended a webinar and remain in nurture; no demo request is recorded.

  1. Lifecycle marketer: These three contacts attended the webinar and remain in nurture. No demonstration request is recorded.
  2. Account executive: Are you handing them to me as sales-qualified leads or sharing engagement context only?
  3. Lifecycle marketer: Engagement context only. Attendance doesn't establish readiness for a sales conversation.
  4. Account executive: Then please don't title the handoff three ready-to-buy accounts.
  5. Lifecycle marketer: Agreed. I'll include the recorded interaction and the limits of what it shows.
  6. Account executive: Who will check whether a later request or relevant restriction exists in the CRM?
  7. Lifecycle marketer: I'll ask marketing operations to verify the current record before any status change.
  8. Account executive: Good. I won't infer a request from the webinar attendance alone.
  9. Lifecycle marketer: I'll return the verified context and distinguish an MQL assessment from any SQL decision.
  10. Account executive: That gives sales useful information without turning a nurture event into an invented buying signal.
A suppression flag stays visible at handoff

Separate fictional CRM handoff: one contact appears on a campaign list and a suppression list; the reason for suppression has not been checked.

  1. CRM specialist: One contact appears in both the campaign list and the suppression list. I'm flagging the conflict.
  2. Campaign coordinator: Can I delete the suppression flag so the list is complete for handoff?
  3. CRM specialist: No. We need to understand the restriction through the appropriate process before any outreach decision.
  4. Campaign coordinator: Do we know why the flag exists, or are we still checking?
  5. CRM specialist: The reason hasn't been checked. I won't invent consent history or assume an error.
  6. Campaign coordinator: Then the handoff should identify the record as requiring review, not as cleared for contact.
  7. CRM specialist: Exactly. I'll provide the internal reference and request the restriction review from the responsible owner.
  8. Campaign coordinator: I'll keep it out of any assumed cleared group while that question remains unresolved.
  9. CRM specialist: Please confirm the boundary when you brief the receiving team.
  10. Campaign coordinator: I'll state that list membership doesn't override the unresolved suppression status or authorize outreach.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

A hundred contacts are not a hundred sales requests
  1. Read the corrected contact handoff. Separate 20 demonstration requests, 60 guide downloads and 20 unknown-source records.
  2. Switch roles. Preserve source verification, permission and suppression checks, documented request and receiving owner as distinct conditions under this company's procedure.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

An export does not renew a preference

A contact is on the company's current suppression list for promotional email. A later event export includes the same address but supplies no new preference information. The team has not reviewed the conflict.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Operator: "The export contains the same ___."

Answer and explanation

B. address

The case identifies one address appearing in both records, not evidence of a new person.

2. Lead: "It does not establish a changed ___."

Answer and explanation

B. preference

The later export supplies no new preference information, so the earlier status cannot be assumed reversed.

3. Operator: "I will preserve the existing suppression ___."

Answer and explanation

D. record

Preserving the current record avoids silently removing a restriction without evidence or review.

4. Lead: "Resolve the conflict through the approved ___."

Answer and explanation

B. process

The supplied facts call for review rather than treating the export as automatic authorization.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

07Analytics, Experimentation, Funnel Reporting, and Executive ReadoutsA higher click rate is not yet a declared winner+

Your goal

Present absolute and relative differences while keeping statistical and commercial conclusions separate.

This lesson in the book, page 58 ↗

A Read the situation

A higher click rate is not yet a declared winner

An email test reports 120 unique clickers among 2,000 delivered messages for A and 140 among 2,000 for B. These are the only supplied results. The random assignment, planned stopping rule, and statistical analysis have not yet been checked. No purchase data are available. Director Anika wants to announce B as a proven winner. Analyst Mateo must explain the observed rates and their difference, then identify the checks required before a stronger claim or broader release decision.

Anika: Marketing director / Mateo: Experimentation analyst

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What are the observed unique clicker rates?

Answer and explanation

C. A: 6%; B: 7%

The rates are 120 divided by 2,000 and 140 divided by 2,000, respectively.

2. What is the absolute difference between those rates?

Answer and explanation

D. 1 percentage point

Seven percent minus six percent equals one percentage point; relative change uses a different calculation.

3. Which conclusion is currently unsupported?

Answer and explanation

A. B is a statistically established and commercially superior winner

The design and statistical checks remain incomplete, and no purchase results establish commercial superiority.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

The observed rates are 6% for A and 7% for B: the absolute difference is one percentage point. Relative to 6%, the increase is about 16.7%. Twenty extra observed clickers, one percentage point, and 16.7% relative lift describe different aspects of the same counts.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
A/B test
A comparison of two variants under a specified experimental design.plan an A/B test
control variant
The reference experience used for comparison.define the control variant
treatment variant
The changed experience whose effect is assessed.describe the treatment variant
randomization
Assignment by a chance-based process intended to support comparable groups.verify randomization
randomization unit
The entity assigned to an experiment condition.choose the randomization unit
sample size
The number of observations or assigned units on a defined basis.determine the sample size
sample ratio mismatch
An unexpected departure from the intended allocation proportions.investigate a sample ratio mismatch
primary metric
The preselected main measure for evaluating an experiment.specify the primary metric
guardrail metric
A measure used to detect unacceptable adverse effects.monitor a guardrail metric
denominator
The quantity by which a numerator is divided.verify the denominator
percentage point
The unit for an absolute difference between percentages.report a percentage-point change
relative lift
Change divided by the baseline value, expressed on a relative basis.calculate relative lift
confidence interval
A range produced by a method with a stated long-run coverage property.report a confidence interval
p-value
Probability, under the null model, of results at least as extreme as observed.interpret the p-value
statistical significance
A result meeting a specified statistical decision criterion.assess statistical significance
practical significance
The size and relevance of an effect for an actual decision.distinguish practical significance
statistical power
Probability of detecting a specified effect under an assumed design.assess statistical power
minimum detectable effect
A target effect size a planned design aims to detect reliably.specify the minimum detectable effect
stopping rule
A planned rule for when an experiment ends or is evaluated.follow the stopping rule
multiple testing
Evaluation of multiple hypotheses, with associated error-control concerns.account for multiple testing
cohort
A group defined by a shared entry period or characteristic.compare like-for-like cohorts
funnel stage
A defined step in a progression toward an outcome.distinguish funnel stages
drop-off
The loss of participants between specified stages.measure stage-to-stage drop-off
executive readout
A concise presentation of findings, limits, and decision implications.prepare the executive readout

Higher observed performance does not itself establish statistical significance or business value. A clicker is not necessarily a purchaser. Missing analysis is not evidence of no effect either: report the observation and the unresolved checks without declaring either certainty or failure.

C Notice the language

Give the clear number before the qualification

An executive can need a short answer without needing an overstated answer. Lead with the observed difference, then say what is not established and which check resolves it. Avoid burying the result under statistical vocabulary or letting a request for decisiveness turn an unfinished analysis into proof.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
State the observation
A recorded 6% and B recorded 7% unique clicker rates.
Name the absolute change
The difference is one percentage point.
Give the relative basis
Relative to A's 6%, the observed increase is about 16.7%.
Limit the verdict
B is higher in this sample; a proven winner is not yet established.
Request the design check
Confirm assignment and the planned stopping rule.
Separate the outcome
We have click data, not purchase or revenue results.
Avoid the opposite error
Unfinished analysis does not prove that there is no effect.
Close with next steps
Finish the design and statistical checks before the stronger claim.
Keep the denominator
Each rate uses 2,000 delivered messages.
Identify the count
B has 20 more observed unique clickers.
Ask for uncertainty
Include the appropriate uncertainty estimate with the result.
Check the metric
Was this the preselected primary measure?
Protect the wider decision
Review relevant adverse outcomes before a broader release.
Keep timing visible
Are both groups measured over the same follow-up period?
Clarify the scope
This result does not describe every future audience.
Summarize for leaders
The observed direction is positive; the decision checks remain open.
6 language and precision notes
Percentage point
Use this for subtraction between two percentages, not for the relative ratio.
Relative to
This phrase names the baseline used in a relative-change calculation.
Observed
This qualifier distinguishes the actual sample result from a population or causal conclusion.
Not yet established
This is different from saying disproved or impossible.
Unique clickers
Count distinct clickers under the reporting method, not repeat clicks. A tracking identifier should not be assumed to prove a distinct human without validation.
Winner
Define the statistical and practical criteria before using the label as a decision.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which sentence reports both forms of change accurately?

Answer and explanation

A. B is one percentage point higher, about 16.7% above A on a relative basis.

The absolute difference is 7% minus 6%; relative lift divides that one-point difference by 6%.

2. Which statement keeps the measured outcome distinct from a business result?

Answer and explanation

D. B has a higher observed unique-clicker rate; purchase outcomes are not supplied.

The numerator counts unique clickers, not orders, revenue or customers. Equal delivery totals do not supply the missing downstream results.

3. What is a justified next step?

Answer and explanation

D. Verify design, stopping rule, and statistical analysis before declaring a proven winner.

Neither certainty nor no effect follows from incomplete checks; the case requires completing them.

4. Which readout is appropriately concise?

Answer and explanation

C. B's observed rate is higher; the statistical and commercial conclusions remain open.

The observed rate can be reported now while its stronger implications remain qualified.

A higher click rate is not yet a declared winner

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Anika: Marketing director / Mateo: Experimentation analyst

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • executive readout

  • percentage point

  1. Anika
    B shows one hundred forty clickers against A's one hundred twenty. I'd like to tell the leadership team B wins and send it to everyone.
  2. Mateo
    We can report the observation first. With a 1 of two thousand delivered messages for each version, A's rate is six percent and B's is seven.
  3. Anika
    I'll say one percent better, then. Is that precise enough, or will readers understand a different calculation from the one we actually have?
  4. Mateo
    Use one 2 for the absolute difference. One percent better can sound like a relative comparison, which uses A's rate as the base.
  5. Anika
    That relative number would be one divided by six, about sixteen point seven percent. It sounds much larger than the difference between six and seven.
  6. Mateo
    That's the 3, not an extra improvement. Put both original rates beside it so the audience can see the size and basis of the same change.
  7. Anika
    Both groups have two thousand delivered messages. Doesn't that show they were comparable, or is there something else you need to verify in the setup?
  8. Mateo
    We still need to verify 4. Equal delivered counts don't tell us how recipients were assigned or whether the reported groups follow the intended design.
  9. Anika
    The team watched the dashboard repeatedly during the send. I don't know whether they stopped because B looked ahead or because the planned endpoint arrived.
  10. Mateo
    We'll check the 5. Monitoring is not itself proof of a problem, but outcome-driven stopping can change the analysis needed to support a conclusion.
  11. Anika
    So twenty extra clickers isn't enough to call it statistically significant just by looking at the totals? I need a clear reason to hold that label.
  12. Mateo
    We haven't completed the analysis for 6. A larger observed count alone doesn't establish that conclusion, and we should not turn an unfinished check into proof of no effect either.
  13. Anika
    The dashboard's green arrow makes it look settled. What can we place beside the rates to show uncertainty once the design has been checked?
  14. Mateo
    An appropriate 7 can help. We don't have one calculated in this report, so I'll add the checked estimate rather than invent bounds for the slide.
  15. Anika
    And even if the click difference holds up, we don't know whether people bought anything. I can't present a click result as additional revenue.
  16. Mateo
    Right. 8 asks whether the effect matters to the decision. We need the relevant business outcomes and costs before calling this commercially superior.
  17. Anika
    Was clicker rate our main measure before the send? I don't want us to choose it now just because it happens to favor B.
  18. Mateo
    I'll confirm the 9 and the other planned measures, including adverse outcomes. We need the original decision criteria, not a selection of the most flattering results.
  19. Anika
    Then today's headline will report six versus seven percent, one percentage point apart, with the design and analysis checks open. No proven-winner label or full-send approval.
  20. Mateo
    That makes a clear 10. I'll name the outstanding checks beneath the observed result, and we'll return to the broader decision with the missing evidence.

Answers and explanations
  1. denominator Turn 2. Each rate divides unique clickers by 2,000 delivered messages; a different denominator would change the metric.
  2. percentage point Turn 4. A percentage point expresses the absolute difference between 7% and 6%, rather than their relative change.
  3. relative lift Turn 6. Relative lift divides the change by A's baseline rate; it does not create a larger absolute difference.
  4. randomization Turn 8. Randomization concerns how units were assigned; equal delivered counts alone do not establish the assignment process.
  5. stopping rule Turn 10. The planned stopping rule matters because outcome-driven early stopping can change how statistical evidence should be interpreted.
  6. statistical significance Turn 12. Statistical significance depends on a specified method and criterion; a positive observed difference alone does not establish it.
  7. confidence interval Turn 14. A confidence interval communicates uncertainty under its method and assumptions; the current briefing supplies no calculated interval.
  8. Practical significance Turn 16. Practical significance concerns decision-relevant magnitude and value; more clicks do not automatically establish more profitable purchases.
  9. primary metric Turn 18. The primary metric is selected for evaluating the experiment; choosing it after seeing favorable results changes the evidential context.
  10. executive readout Turn 20. An executive readout gives the observed finding, its limits, and decision implications without converting incomplete analysis into proof.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

One percentage point with significance still pending

The lesson's email test records A: 120 clicks from 2,000 deliveries; B: 140 from 2,000. Significance analysis is incomplete.

  1. Experiment analyst: Version A has a six-percent click rate; B has seven percent, from two thousand deliveries each.
  2. Marketing director: Then can we announce B as the proven winner of the experiment?
  3. Experiment analyst: Not yet. The observed difference is one percentage point, and significance analysis remains incomplete.
  4. Marketing director: What part of the report can we confidently share today?
  5. Experiment analyst: The supplied counts, delivered-message denominator, and observed rates, clearly separated from the pending inference.
  6. Marketing director: Could we call the change a one-percent relative increase in CTR?
  7. Experiment analyst: No. It's one percentage point; the relative increase from six to seven is about sixteen-point-seven percent.
  8. Marketing director: I'll use the correct description and avoid calling the result conclusive.
  9. Experiment analyst: I'll complete the planned checks and report the uncertainty before recommending a rollout.
  10. Marketing director: Good. A measured difference is progress, but it isn't the finished experiment conclusion.
A cohort report with a shorter observation window

Separate fictional funnel report: one signup cohort has thirty days of follow-up, another only ten; final conversion comparison is pending.

  1. Growth manager: The newer cohort has fewer purchases. Can we report that its conversion performance is worse?
  2. Analytics lead: It has only ten days of follow-up, while the older cohort has thirty.
  3. Growth manager: Then the data collection is at different stages, not a completed matched-window comparison.
  4. Analytics lead: Correct. We can report observed activity, but the unequal observation periods limit the conclusion.
  5. Growth manager: Could we compare the first ten days of both cohorts if that data is available?
  6. Analytics lead: That would align the window, but availability and other differences still need checking.
  7. Growth manager: I'll label the newer cohort as still maturing rather than a confirmed failure.
  8. Analytics lead: Please keep the actual counts visible; we don't need to hide incomplete results.
  9. Growth manager: The pending action is a matched-window check, not an automatic campaign change.
  10. Analytics lead: Exactly. We'll distinguish the available observations from the analysis needed to interpret them.
A funnel count waits for duplicate review

Separate fictional analytics exercise: a dashboard counts 300 form submissions; duplicate-person checks have not been completed.

  1. Executive reporting lead: The dashboard shows three hundred submissions. May I call that three hundred new people in the funnel?
  2. Marketing analyst: Not yet. We haven't checked whether some people submitted more than once.
  3. Executive reporting lead: So submission events and unique people are different measures, even if the number looks useful.
  4. Marketing analyst: Exactly. Calling events people would overstate what the completed counting step establishes.
  5. Executive reporting lead: Does that make the submission count a vanity metric we should discard entirely?
  6. Marketing analyst: Not necessarily. It can serve a purpose if labeled correctly and linked to the question we're answering.
  7. Executive reporting lead: I'll show submissions now and mark the unique-person calculation as pending.
  8. Marketing analyst: Good. The duplicate review should use a defined method rather than remove records arbitrarily.
  9. Executive reporting lead: Then we'll update the funnel readout when that check is complete.
  10. Marketing analyst: Yes, and explain any revised count instead of silently changing what the original metric meant.

Two scenarios to practice

A higher click rate is not yet a declared winner
  1. Read the corrected test discussion. Give 6% for A, 7% for B, one percentage point and about 16.7% relative lift using the stated denominators.
  2. Switch roles. Keep assignment, stopping rule and analysis checks open; neither a proven winner nor no effect is established.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A bigger numerator, a lower rate

Campaign C receives 90 requests from 1,000 visits. Campaign D receives 100 requests from 2,000 visits. These are observed totals, not a controlled test.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Analyst: "C converts at ___ percent."

Answer and explanation

C. nine

Dividing 90 requests by 1,000 visits gives 9 percent.

2. Lead: "D converts at ___ percent."

Answer and explanation

A. five

Dividing 100 requests by 2,000 visits gives 5 percent despite the larger request count.

3. Analyst: "D has more requests but a lower ___."

Answer and explanation

A. rate

The count and rate move in different directions because D has twice as many visits.

4. Lead: "The totals do not establish a causal ___."

Answer and explanation

B. effect

The supplied comparison is observational rather than a controlled design isolating a campaign effect.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Lesson 07: Analytics, Experimentation, Funnel Reporting, and Executive Readouts
Original fictional case: An email test reports 120 unique clickers among 2,000 delivered messages for A and 140 among 2,000 for B. These are the only supplied results. The random assignment, planned stopping rule, and statistical analysis have not yet been checked. No purchase data are available. Director Anika wants to announce B as a proven winner. Analyst Mateo must explain the observed rates and their difference, then identify the checks required before a stronger claim or broader release decision.
Language workshop: A higher click rate is not yet a declared winner
Communication goal: Present absolute and relative differences while keeping statistical and commercial conclusions separate.
Language guidance: The observed rates are 6% for A and 7% for B: the absolute difference is one percentage point. Relative to 6%, the increase is about 16.7%. Twenty extra observed clickers, one percentage point, and 16.7% relative lift describe different aspects of the same counts.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): A recorded 6% and B recorded 7% unique clicker rates. / The difference is one percentage point. / Relative to A's 6%, the observed increase is about 16.7%. / B is higher in this sample; a proven winner is not yet established. / Confirm assignment and the planned stopping rule. / We have click data, not purchase or revenue results. / Unfinished analysis does not prove that there is no effect. / Finish the design and statistical checks before the stronger claim. / Each rate uses 2,000 delivered messages. / B has 20 more observed unique clickers. / Include the appropriate uncertainty estimate with the result. / Was this the preselected primary measure? / Review relevant adverse outcomes before a broader release. / Are both groups measured over the same follow-up period? / This result does not describe every future audience. / The observed direction is positive; the decision checks remain open.
Vocabulary: A/B test: A comparison of two variants under a specified experimental design. / control variant: The reference experience used for comparison. / treatment variant: The changed experience whose effect is assessed. / randomization: Assignment by a chance-based process intended to support comparable groups. / randomization unit: The entity assigned to an experiment condition. / sample size: The number of observations or assigned units on a defined basis. / sample ratio mismatch: An unexpected departure from the intended allocation proportions. / primary metric: The preselected main measure for evaluating an experiment. / guardrail metric: A measure used to detect unacceptable adverse effects. / denominator: The quantity by which a numerator is divided. / percentage point: The unit for an absolute difference between percentages. / relative lift: Change divided by the baseline value, expressed on a relative basis. / confidence interval: A range produced by a method with a stated long-run coverage property. / p-value: Probability, under the null model, of results at least as extreme as observed. / statistical significance: A result meeting a specified statistical decision criterion. / practical significance: The size and relevance of an effect for an actual decision. / statistical power: Probability of detecting a specified effect under an assumed design. / minimum detectable effect: A target effect size a planned design aims to detect reliably. / stopping rule: A planned rule for when an experiment ends or is evaluated. / multiple testing: Evaluation of multiple hypotheses, with associated error-control concerns. / cohort: A group defined by a shared entry period or characteristic. / funnel stage: A defined step in a progression toward an outcome. / drop-off: The loss of participants between specified stages. / executive readout: A concise presentation of findings, limits, and decision implications.
Speaking task: Read the corrected test discussion. Give 6% for A, 7% for B, one percentage point and about 16.7% relative lift using the stated denominators. Switch roles. Keep assignment, stopping rule and analysis checks open; neither a proven winner nor no effect is established. Read the corrected transfer. Contrast C's 90 requests at 9% with D's 100 at 5%, without making a causal claim.
Partner: Anika: Marketing director / Mateo: Experimentation analyst

Mateo: I'll confirm the primary metric and the other planned measures, including adverse outcomes. We need the original decision criteria, not a selection of the most flattering results.
Anika: Then today's headline will report six versus seven percent, one percentage point apart, with the design and analysis checks open. No proven-winner label or full-send approval.
Mateo: That makes a clear executive readout. I'll name the outstanding checks beneath the observed result, and we'll return to the broader decision with the missing evidence.
END REFERENCE

Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Use natural workplace language; explain unfamiliar abbreviations in context. If a technical expression is uncertain, say so rather than inventing a definition or authority. Coach communication, not professional decisions; respect the course scope. Ask only for fictional or anonymized practice details. Judge clarity, meaning, appropriate tone and the next step. Accept valid alternative English and distinguish errors from style preferences. Do not claim to certify my language level. Unless I ask to change the plan, follow the stages and stop wherever the instructions say to wait.

REFERENCE
Course: Marketing English
Professional audience: brand, product marketing, growth, content, SEO, lifecycle, demand generation, marketing operations, social, and agency teams
Scope: Fictional English-language practice, not legal advice or a promise of campaign results. Legal requirements, platform policies, and data permissions depend on context and location. Obtain current qualified review for actual claims, audience data, disclosures, and publication decisions.
Lesson 07: Analytics, Experimentation, Funnel Reporting, and Executive Readouts
Original fictional case: An email test reports 120 unique clickers among 2,000 delivered messages for A and 140 among 2,000 for B. These are the only supplied results. The random assignment, planned stopping rule, and statistical analysis have not yet been checked. No purchase data are available. Director Anika wants to announce B as a proven winner. Analyst Mateo must explain the observed rates and their difference, then identify the checks required before a stronger claim or broader release decision.
Language workshop: A higher click rate is not yet a declared winner
Communication goal: Present absolute and relative differences while keeping statistical and commercial conclusions separate.
Language guidance: The observed rates are 6% for A and 7% for B: the absolute difference is one percentage point. Relative to 6%, the increase is about 16.7%. Twenty extra observed clickers, one percentage point, and 16.7% relative lift describe different aspects of the same counts.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): A recorded 6% and B recorded 7% unique clicker rates. / The difference is one percentage point. / Relative to A's 6%, the observed increase is about 16.7%. / B is higher in this sample; a proven winner is not yet established. / Confirm assignment and the planned stopping rule. / We have click data, not purchase or revenue results. / Unfinished analysis does not prove that there is no effect. / Finish the design and statistical checks before the stronger claim. / Each rate uses 2,000 delivered messages. / B has 20 more observed unique clickers. / Include the appropriate uncertainty estimate with the result. / Was this the preselected primary measure? / Review relevant adverse outcomes before a broader release. / Are both groups measured over the same follow-up period? / This result does not describe every future audience. / The observed direction is positive; the decision checks remain open.
Vocabulary: A/B test: A comparison of two variants under a specified experimental design. / control variant: The reference experience used for comparison. / treatment variant: The changed experience whose effect is assessed. / randomization: Assignment by a chance-based process intended to support comparable groups. / randomization unit: The entity assigned to an experiment condition. / sample size: The number of observations or assigned units on a defined basis. / sample ratio mismatch: An unexpected departure from the intended allocation proportions. / primary metric: The preselected main measure for evaluating an experiment. / guardrail metric: A measure used to detect unacceptable adverse effects. / denominator: The quantity by which a numerator is divided. / percentage point: The unit for an absolute difference between percentages. / relative lift: Change divided by the baseline value, expressed on a relative basis. / confidence interval: A range produced by a method with a stated long-run coverage property. / p-value: Probability, under the null model, of results at least as extreme as observed. / statistical significance: A result meeting a specified statistical decision criterion. / practical significance: The size and relevance of an effect for an actual decision. / statistical power: Probability of detecting a specified effect under an assumed design. / minimum detectable effect: A target effect size a planned design aims to detect reliably. / stopping rule: A planned rule for when an experiment ends or is evaluated. / multiple testing: Evaluation of multiple hypotheses, with associated error-control concerns. / cohort: A group defined by a shared entry period or characteristic. / funnel stage: A defined step in a progression toward an outcome. / drop-off: The loss of participants between specified stages. / executive readout: A concise presentation of findings, limits, and decision implications.
Speaking task: Read the corrected test discussion. Give 6% for A, 7% for B, one percentage point and about 16.7% relative lift using the stated denominators. Switch roles. Keep assignment, stopping rule and analysis checks open; neither a proven winner nor no effect is established. Read the corrected transfer. Contrast C's 90 requests at 9% with D's 100 at 5%, without making a causal claim.
Partner: Anika: Marketing director / Mateo: Experimentation analyst
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: Campaign C receives 90 requests from 1,000 visits. Campaign D receives 100 requests from 2,000 visits. These are observed totals, not a controlled test.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Anika: Was clicker rate our main measure before the send? I don't want us to choose it now just because it happens to favor B.
Mateo: I'll confirm the primary metric and the other planned measures, including adverse outcomes. We need the original decision criteria, not a selection of the most flattering results.
Anika: Then today's headline will report six versus seven percent, one percentage point apart, with the design and analysis checks open. No proven-winner label or full-send approval.
Mateo: That makes a clear executive readout. I'll name the outstanding checks beneath the observed result, and we'll return to the broader decision with the missing evidence.
END REFERENCE

Your goal

Coordinate a publication hold, preserve review evidence, and communicate only verified status.

This lesson in the book, page 67 ↗

A Read the situation

Stopping a scheduled claim before it goes live

A social post scheduled for 3 p.m. says a product is "100% private." The reviewer has requested revised wording and supporting evidence; approval is pending. A paid creator has received the same draft asset, but their publication status is unknown. No privacy incident has been reported in the case. Social lead Noor can pause the company queue, and campaign lead Caleb owns partner coordination. They must prevent unapproved publication, verify the partner's status, and keep a clear record without announcing an incident or clearance that has not been established.

Noor: Social-media lead / Caleb: Campaign lead

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is the company post's current approval state?

Answer and explanation

D. Pending, with wording and evidence changes requested

The reviewer has requested changes and supporting evidence, so scheduling does not establish approval.

2. What is unknown?

Answer and explanation

D. Whether the paid creator has published the draft

The briefing specifically leaves the partner's publication status unverified.

3. Which statement would invent a fact?

Answer and explanation

D. A confirmed privacy incident has occurred

The case explicitly supplies no reported privacy incident, so one must not be announced as established.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Scheduled, approved, and published name different states. Pausing the company queue controls that queue; it does not prove what a partner has done. Record the exact asset, recipient, request, and confirmation rather than saying "everything is stopped" before verification.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
publication hold
An instruction or control stopping release pending a condition.place a publication hold
approval workflow
The sequence of review and authorization steps for release.follow the approval workflow
claims register
A record of claims, evidence, owners, and review status.update the claims register
absolute claim
A statement using an unrestricted expression such as always or completely.review an absolute claim
material connection
A relationship that may affect how an endorsement is evaluated.disclose a material connection
sponsored content
Content produced or distributed as part of a commercial arrangement.identify sponsored content
endorsement
A promotional message expressing another party's opinion or experience.review an endorsement
disclosure
Information made available to clarify a relevant fact or relationship.assess the disclosure
usage rights
Permissions governing how content or an asset may be used.verify usage rights
release form
A document recording permission for a specified use or participation.check the release form
brand safety
Measures intended to avoid harmful advertising contexts.review brand safety
brand suitability
The fit of a placement with a particular brand's standards.assess brand suitability
exclusion list
Defined placements or categories barred from a campaign.maintain an exclusion list
personal data
Information relating to an identifiable person under the applicable framework.protect personal data
data minimization
Limiting collected or shared data to what is needed for the purpose.apply data minimization
purpose limitation
Restricting data use to appropriate specified purposes.check purpose limitation
retention period
The time for which information is kept under applicable requirements.confirm the retention period
access control
Rules limiting who can view or change information.enforce access control
incident triage
Initial assessment and routing of a reported event.begin incident triage
holding statement
An initial message limited to verified facts while review continues.prepare a holding statement
correction notice
A communication identifying and correcting an earlier error.issue a correction notice
takedown request
A request to remove published material.send a takedown request
escalation path
The designated route for raising an issue to the appropriate authority.use the escalation path
audit trail
A traceable record of actions, decisions, and changes.preserve the audit trail

A disclosure of payment does not establish the truth of a product claim. Likewise, a review concern is not proof of a privacy incident. Keep the commercial relationship, claim evidence, publication status, and incident status as separate questions.

C Notice the language

Use firm operational language without inventing a crisis

A pending review can justify a publication hold without proving a product failure. Name the exact asset and action required. Keep "requested," "confirmed," and "approved" separate so that a message to a partner does not become mistaken evidence that every copy has been stopped.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Name the release state
The asset is scheduled, but approval is still pending.
Give a precise hold
Pause this version in the company queue now.
Check the partner
Please confirm whether this exact asset has been published.
Preserve the evidence
Keep the draft, reviewer comments, and action history.
Limit the announcement
We have a claim-review issue, not a confirmed privacy incident.
Separate disclosure
A sponsorship disclosure does not substantiate the product claim.
Control the revision
Use only the version approved through the review workflow.
Close with confirmation
Record each hold request and the confirmation received.
Assign coordination
I will contact the partner and track their response.
Avoid overstatement
We have paused our queue; the partner's status remains unverified.
Scope a response
The statement should include only facts we have checked.
Protect private details
Move personal information into the approved restricted channel.
Check permission
Confirm the agreed usage rights before reusing the creator's asset.
Escalate specifically
The unresolved claim needs the designated review owner.
Distinguish removal
A takedown request is not confirmation that every copy is gone.
Release carefully
Resume publication only after the required approvals and version checks.
6 language and precision notes
Pause and withdraw
Pause stops a planned release; removing already published material is a different action.
Requested and confirmed
These words distinguish an instruction from evidence that it was carried out.
Same asset
Use an exact version identifier so partners do not act on a different file.
No confirmed incident
This limits what is known without asserting that a review can never find an issue.
Disclosure and proof
A relationship disclosure answers who is connected, not whether the product claim is true.
Only verified facts
This limits a holding statement while investigation or review remains unfinished.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which immediate update is accurate after Noor pauses the queue?

Answer and explanation

B. Our queue is paused; the partner's publication status still needs confirmation.

Pausing one controlled queue establishes only that action, not partner status, incident facts, or claim approval.

2. Which message to the creator resolves the immediate release uncertainty?

Answer and explanation

B. Hold this exact draft and confirm whether it has already been published.

The unapproved version needs a hold and a publication-status check. Disclosure and contract records answer different questions; replacement wording also needs review.

3. Which statement correctly separates two review issues?

Answer and explanation

C. Disclosing sponsorship does not prove the product claim.

The commercial relationship and the evidence for the product assertion are distinct questions.

4. What belongs in the action record?

Answer and explanation

B. Asset version, review comments, hold requests, confirmations, and responsible owners

A traceable record preserves what was requested, what is verified, and who must resolve the remaining work.

Answers and explanations
  1. publication hold Turn 2. A publication hold stops the unapproved release while the requested claim review remains unresolved.
  2. escalation path Turn 4. The escalation path identifies the responsible route for urgent partner coordination; it does not assume the partner has already acted.
  3. audit trail Turn 6. The audit trail records the draft, review concern, and actions; deleting it would remove evidence needed to understand the decision.
  4. absolute claim Turn 8. An absolute claim leaves little or no qualification; substituting another unrestricted promise would not resolve the evidence gap.
  5. material connection Turn 10. A material connection concerns the relationship behind an endorsement; disclosing it does not substantiate the separate product assertion.
  6. holding statement Turn 12. A holding statement should stay within verified facts; an unresolved claim review does not establish a privacy incident.
  7. takedown request Turn 14. A takedown request concerns already published content; sending it is not proof that removal has occurred everywhere.
  8. usage rights Turn 16. Usage rights define permitted uses of the creator's assets; access to a file does not establish unrestricted reuse.
  9. data minimization Turn 18. Data minimization keeps unnecessary personal details out of the public communication while preserving relevant information in the appropriate record.
  10. approval workflow Turn 20. The approval workflow controls review and authorization of the revised version before publication resumes.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Correcting a scheduled claim before publication

The lesson's scheduled post contains a claim reviewers asked to revise; it has not been published.

  1. Social media coordinator: The scheduled post still contains the claim reviewers asked us to revise. It hasn't been published.
  2. Brand safety lead: Then we need to correct the draft status and prevent publication of that unreviewed wording.
  3. Social media coordinator: I described it as approved in the handoff. That was inaccurate, and I'll correct the message.
  4. Brand safety lead: Good. Keep the substantiation question visible rather than imply approval occurred.
  5. Social media coordinator: Should I announce that customers have already seen a false claim?
  6. Brand safety lead: No. The supplied fact is that the post is unpublished, not a confirmed public exposure.
  7. Social media coordinator: I'll ask the publishing owner to confirm the hold and route revised wording for review.
  8. Brand safety lead: Please distinguish requesting a hold from a confirmed scheduling change.
  9. Social media coordinator: I'll report the actual status after that check and avoid claiming the issue resolved prematurely.
  10. Brand safety lead: Exactly. The correction should preserve both the review requirement and the publication facts.
A creator relationship omitted from the brief

Separate fictional campaign exercise: a creator receives a free product, but the draft brief says there is no material connection. Nothing has been published.

  1. Creator partnerships manager: The brief says no material connection, but the creator receives a free product in this campaign.
  2. Compliance reviewer: Then the brief's description of the relationship is inaccurate and needs correction before publication review.
  3. Creator partnerships manager: Can we ignore the product because no cash payment is involved in the supplied arrangement?
  4. Compliance reviewer: Don't assume that removes relevance. The actual relationship needs review under the applicable requirements.
  5. Creator partnerships manager: I'll replace the no-connection claim with a factual description of the free product.
  6. Compliance reviewer: Good. Avoid inventing a universal disclosure formula or claiming the revised wording is legally approved.
  7. Creator partnerships manager: The content is still unpublished, so I won't describe this as a completed public violation.
  8. Compliance reviewer: Correct. Ask the responsible reviewer to assess the appropriate communication before release.
  9. Creator partnerships manager: I'll document the brief correction and keep approval status pending.
  10. Compliance reviewer: Then the review starts from accurate facts rather than a misleading compensation assumption.
An image-use assumption needs correction

Separate fictional marketing exercise: a draft uses a customer photo because it appeared on a public website; permission for this use has not been checked.

  1. Content producer: I marked the customer photo cleared because it was visible on a public website.
  2. Marketing reviewer: Public visibility doesn't establish permission for our proposed use. That clearance claim needs correction.
  3. Content producer: The draft hasn't been released. I'll state that permission is unverified rather than already granted.
  4. Marketing reviewer: Good. Keep the consent or rights question with the appropriate review owner.
  5. Content producer: Could we assume the customer would welcome the exposure and publish while we ask?
  6. Marketing reviewer: No. Their likely reaction isn't evidence of authorization, and we shouldn't invent consent.
  7. Content producer: I'll remove the cleared label and request an approved asset or a completed permission check.
  8. Marketing reviewer: Please confirm the draft's actual status before describing any public use or harm.
  9. Content producer: I'll report only the unverified draft use and the corrective step being requested.
  10. Marketing reviewer: That preserves the facts and gives the publishing team a clear unresolved condition.

Vocabulary: publication hold: An instruction or control stopping release pending a condition. / approval workflow: The sequence of review and authorization steps for release. / claims register: A record of claims, evidence, owners, and review status. / absolute claim: A statement using an unrestricted expression such as always or completely. / material connection: A relationship that may affect how an endorsement is evaluated. / sponsored content: Content produced or distributed as part of a commercial arrangement. / endorsement: A promotional message expressing another party's opinion or experience. / disclosure: Information made available to clarify a relevant fact or relationship. / usage rights: Permissions governing how content or an asset may be used. / release form: A document recording permission for a specified use or participation. / brand safety: Measures intended to avoid harmful advertising contexts. / brand suitability: The fit of a placement with a particular brand's standards. / exclusion list: Defined placements or categories barred from a campaign. / personal data: Information relating to an identifiable person under the applicable framework. / data minimization: Limiting collected or shared data to what is needed for the purpose. / purpose limitation: Restricting data use to appropriate specified purposes. / retention period: The time for which information is kept under applicable requirements. / access control: Rules limiting who can view or change information. / incident triage: Initial assessment and routing of a reported event. / holding statement: An initial message limited to verified facts while review continues. / correction notice: A communication identifying and correcting an earlier error. / takedown request: A request to remove published material. / escalation path: The designated route for raising an issue to the appropriate authority. / audit trail: A traceable record of actions, decisions, and changes.

Practice grammar in context — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Choose grammar that preserves the meaning
1. Use the lesson's language workshop, or one actual sentence from the dialogue, to explain a single grammar distinction in no more than 90 words. Show how it affects timing, certainty, responsibility or politeness.
2. Give one brief occupational exchange containing a gap and four complete options A-D. Supply enough context for exactly one answer. Keep distractors plausible; distinguish grammar errors from wording that changes the facts. Stop and wait.
3. Explain why each choice fits or fails, then ask me to read the completed exchange aloud. Do not request a draft, original written sentence or essay.
4. Repeat with three new exchanges, one at a time, moving from recognition to a more subtle meaning contrast. Do not copy the published checks. Label invented variations and do not turn uncertainty into a promise.
5. End with a short contrast table and two supported spoken turns using supplied frames. Accept accurate alternatives in oral practice; acknowledge and replace ambiguous multiple-choice items.

Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.
